vjimc-2013-cat2-01.title: Compare with the sum of odd numbers
vjimc-2013-cat2-01.body:
Let $p_1=2,p_2=3,\dots$ be the primes, so $S_{n+1}=S_n+p_{n+1}$.

**Reduction.** If $\sqrt{S_{n+1}}-\sqrt{S_n}>1$, the open interval $(\sqrt{S_n},\sqrt{S_{n+1}})$ contains an integer $m$, and then $S_n<m^2<S_{n+1}$. Since $(\sqrt{S_n}+1)^2=S_n+2\sqrt{S_n}+1$, it suffices to show
$$p_{n+1}>1+2\sqrt{S_n}. \tag{1}$$

**Small $n$.** $S_1=2,S_2=5,S_3=10,S_4=17,S_5=28$, and $4\in(2,5)$, $9\in(5,10)$, $16\in(10,17)$, $25\in(17,28)$. So the claim holds for $n\le4$.

**$n\ge5$.** Then $p_n\ge11$. The sum $1+3+5+\dots+p_n$ of all odd numbers up to $p_n$ contains every odd prime $\le p_n$ and also $1$ and $9$; since $2<1+9$,
$$S_n=2+\sum_{3\le p\le p_n}p<1+3+5+\dots+p_n=\left(\frac{p_n+1}{2}\right)^2 .$$
Hence $2\sqrt{S_n}<p_n+1$. As $p_n$ and $p_{n+1}$ are both odd, $p_{n+1}\ge p_n+2>2\sqrt{S_n}+1$, which is (1). ∎

vjimc-2013-cat2-02.title: Coordinates of an intersection point
vjimc-2013-cat2-02.body:
**Answer: $3^n-2^n-n2^{n-1}$.**

Take the cube $[0,1]^n$, with vertices in $\{0,1\}^n$. For a segment $[u,v]$ between vertices let $D(u,v)=\{i:u_i\ne v_i\}\ne\emptyset$. The point $P=u+t(v-u)$ has $P_i=u_i\in\{0,1\}$ for $i\notin D$, and $P_i\in\{t,1-t\}$ for $i\in D$.

**Claim.** If two different segments $[u,v]$ and $[w,z]$ meet at a point $P$ that is not a vertex, then $P$ is the midpoint of both.

*Proof.* Write $P=u+t(v-u)=w+s(z-w)$. As $P$ is not a vertex, $t,s\in(0,1)$. If $i\in D(u,v)\setminus D(w,z)$, then $P_i\in\{t,1-t\}\cap\{0,1\}=\emptyset$ — impossible; so $D(u,v)=D(w,z)=:D$. If $t\ne\frac12$, then from $P$ we can recover the segment: outside $D$, $u$ and $v$ agree with $P$; on $D$, $u_i=0,v_i=1$ where $P_i=t$, and $u_i=1,v_i=0$ where $P_i=1-t$. Since $\{s,1-s\}=\{t,1-t\}$ (both equal the set of values of $P$ on $D$, as $D\ne\emptyset$ and $t\ne1-t$), the same recipe recovers $\{w,z\}=\{u,v\}$ — contradicting that the segments are different. Hence $t=\frac12$, and likewise $s=\frac12$. $\square$

So every intersection point is a point $P\in\{0,\frac12,1\}^n$, and $D$ is the set of coordinates where $P_i=\frac12$. Conversely, given $P\in\{0,\frac12,1\}^n$ with $|D|=m\ge1$ coordinates equal to $\frac12$, the segments having $P$ as midpoint are exactly the $[u,v]$ with $u,v$ equal to $P$ off $D$ and complementary on $D$: there are $2^{m-1}$ of them. Two different such segments exist iff $m\ge2$, and then they meet at $P$, which is not a vertex.

**Count.** Points of $\{0,\frac12,1\}^n$ with at least two coordinates $\frac12$:
$$3^n-\underbrace{2^n}_{\text{no }1/2}-\underbrace{n2^{n-1}}_{\text{exactly one }1/2}.$$
(Checks: $n=2$: $1$, the centre; $n=3$: $7$, six face centres and the centre.) ∎

vjimc-2013-cat2-03.title: Reduce modulo the minimal polynomial
vjimc-2013-cat2-03.body:
Let $\alpha=\sqrt[3]5$ and $x_0=\alpha+\alpha^2$.

**Facts.** (i) $1,\alpha,\alpha^2$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb Q$: $\alpha$ is a root of $x^3-5$, which is irreducible over $\mathbb Q$ (Eisenstein at $5$), so $\alpha$ is not a root of any nonzero rational polynomial of degree $\le2$.
(ii) $x_0^2=\alpha^2+2\alpha^3+\alpha^4=10+5\alpha+\alpha^2$, and
$$x_0^3=\alpha^3+3\alpha^4+3\alpha^5+\alpha^6=5+15\alpha+15\alpha^2+25=30+15x_0,$$
so $x_0$ is a root of the monic integer polynomial $Q(x)=x^3-15x-30$.

**Reduction.** Suppose $P\in\mathbb Z[x]$ with $P(x_0)=5+\alpha$. Since $Q$ is monic, division with remainder stays in $\mathbb Z[x]$: $P=QR+w$ with $R,w\in\mathbb Z[x]$, $\deg w\le2$. Then $w(x_0)=P(x_0)=5+\alpha$.

**The remainder is forced.** Write $w=ax^2+bx+c$. By (ii),
$$w(x_0)=a(10+5\alpha+\alpha^2)+b(\alpha+\alpha^2)+c=(10a+c)+(5a+b)\alpha+(a+b)\alpha^2 .$$
By (i), $w(x_0)=5+\alpha$ forces
$$10a+c=5,\qquad5a+b=1,\qquad a+b=0,$$
so $a=\frac14$, $b=-\frac14$, $c=\frac52$ — not integers. Contradiction; no such $P$ exists. ∎

vjimc-2013-cat2-04.title: Apply the Abel transform once more
vjimc-2013-cat2-04.body:
**Answer: $\dfrac2\pi$.**

**Lemma.** For continuous $f$ on $[0,1]$,
$$\int_0^1\left(\int_0^x\frac{f(t)}{\sqrt{x-t}}\,dt\right)\frac{dx}{\sqrt{1-x}}=\pi\int_0^1f(t)\,dt .$$
*Proof.* The integrand $\frac{|f(t)|}{\sqrt{x-t}\sqrt{1-x}}$ on $0<t<x<1$ is integrable (see below), so by Fubini we may swap the order:
$$\int_0^1f(t)\left(\int_t^1\frac{dx}{\sqrt{(x-t)(1-x)}}\right)dt .$$
For $t<1$, substitute $x=t+(1-t)\sin^2\varphi$, $\varphi\in[0,\frac\pi2]$: then $x-t=(1-t)\sin^2\varphi$, $1-x=(1-t)\cos^2\varphi$, $dx=2(1-t)\sin\varphi\cos\varphi\,d\varphi$, and the inner integral is $\int_0^{\pi/2}2\,d\varphi=\pi$. This also shows the absolute integral is $\pi\int_0^1|f|<\infty$. $\square$

**Upper bound.** For $f\in\mathcal F$ the inner integral in the lemma has absolute value $\le1$, so
$$\left|\int_0^1f\right|\le\frac1\pi\int_0^1\frac{dx}{\sqrt{1-x}}=\frac2\pi .$$

**The bound is approached.** The function $g(t)=\frac{1}{\pi\sqrt t}$ satisfies, by the same substitution $t=x\sin^2\varphi$,
$$\int_0^x\frac{g(t)}{\sqrt{x-t}}\,dt=\frac1\pi\int_0^x\frac{dt}{\sqrt{t(x-t)}}=1,$$
but it is not continuous at $0$. Take $f_n(t)=\frac{1}{\pi\sqrt{t+1/n}}$: continuous on $[0,1]$, $0<f_n<g$, so
$$0<\int_0^x\frac{f_n(t)}{\sqrt{x-t}}\,dt<\int_0^x\frac{g(t)}{\sqrt{x-t}}\,dt=1,$$
i.e. $f_n\in\mathcal F$. And
$$\int_0^1f_n=\frac2\pi\left(\sqrt{1+\tfrac1n}-\sqrt{\tfrac1n}\right)\longrightarrow\frac2\pi .$$
Hence the supremum equals $\dfrac2\pi$ (it is not attained). ∎
